chunk-003.context:
The following section details Chapter 2: Technical Performance, Section 2.1: Overview of AI in 2024, from the AI Index Report. The AI Index Steering Committee selected the most notable model and dataset releases of 2024. The chronological timeline below lists each release's date, name, category, creator, and significance, along with accompanying figure source attributions:

- January 19, 2024: Stable LM 2 (LLM, Stability AI). Stability's latest language model builds on the original Stable LM with enhanced performance. At 1.6 billion parameters, it is designed to run efficiently on portable devices like laptops and smartphones. (Figure 2.1.1, Source: Wikipedia, 2025)
- February 8, 2024: Aya Dataset (Dataset, Cohere for AI/Beijing Academy of AI/Cohere/Binghamton University). A collection of 513 million prompt-completion pairs spanning 114 languages, released as part of Cohere's Aya initiative. The accompanying paper and dataset represent significant milestones in multilingual instruction tuning. (Figure 2.1.2, Source: Cohere, 2025)
- February 15, 2024: Gemini 1.5 Pro (LLM, Google DeepMind). Google's Gemini model set a new benchmark with a 1M token context window, far exceeding GPT-4 Turbo's 128K token limit. (Figure 2.1.3, Source: Google, 2024)
- February 20, 2024: SDXL-Lightning (Text-to-image, ByteDance). Developed by TikTok's creators, this model was among the fastest text-to-image systems at release, generating high-quality synthetic images in under a second using progressive adversarial distillation instead of diffusion-based techniques. (Figure 2.1.4, Source: Hugging Face, 2025)
- February 20, 2024: Claude 3 (LLM, Anthropic). Anthropic's latest LLM outperforms GPT-4 and Gemini on nearly all industry benchmarks, reduces incorrect prompt refusals, and delivers significantly higher accuracy. (Figure 2.1.5, Source: Anthropic, 2025)
- March 7, 2024: Inflection-2.5 (LLM, Inflection AI). Inflection's flagship product "Pi" featured an exceptional model with GPT-4–level performance while using only 40% of its computing resources. Microsoft acquired Inflection for $650 million just two weeks after release. (Figure 2.1.6, Source: Inflection, 2025)
- March 19, 2024: Moirai and LOTSA (Model/dataset, Salesforce). Salesforce unveiled Moirai, a foundation model for universal forecasting, alongside LOTSA, a diverse, large-scale time series dataset with 27 billion observations spanning nine domains. (Figure 2.1.7, Source: Salesforce, 2025)
- March 27, 2024: DBRX (LLM, Databricks). Databricks' open-source mixture-of-experts (MoE) LLM is a fine-grained model that surpasses similar small MoE models like Mixtral and Grok. This transformer decoder-only model features 132B parameters (36B active per input) and was trained on 12 trillion tokens. (Figure 2.1.8, Source: Databricks, 2025)
- April 2, 2024: Stable Audio 2 (Text-to-song and song-to-song, Stability AI). The latest version of Stable Audio now supports audio-to-audio functionality, allowing users to upload songs and manipulate them using natural language prompts. (Figure 2.1.9, Source: Stability AI, 2025)
- April 17, 2024: Llama 3 (LLM, Meta). The Llama 3 series debuts with 8B and 70B parameter text-based models, ranking among the highest performing models of their size to date. (Figure 2.1.10, Source: Meta, 2025)
- May 13, 2024: GPT-4o (Multimodal, OpenAI). A new multimodal model capable of processing inputs in any combination of text, audio, images, and video, and generating outputs in the same formats. It responds to audio in as little as 320 milliseconds, matching human response times. (Figure 2.1.11, Source: OpenAI, 2024)
- June 7, 2024: Qwen2 (LLM, Alibaba). Developed by China's Alibaba, Qwen2 is a series of advanced base and instruction-tuned models that rival competitors like Llama 3-70B and Mixtral-8x22B in performance across numerous benchmarks. (Figure 2.1.12, Source: Qwen, 2024)
- June 17, 2024: Runway Gen-3 (Text-to-video and image-to-video, Runway). Runway's upgraded video generation model excels at creating photorealistic humans with vivid and expressive emotionality. (Figure 2.1.13, Source: Runway, 2024)
- July 23, 2024: Llama 3.1 405B (LLM, Meta). Meta's largest model to date and final entry in the Llama 3.1 family, featuring 405B parameters. It became the most capable openly available foundation model upon release, rivaling many closed models across benchmarks. (Figure 2.1.14, Source: Meta, 2024)
- August 12, 2024: Falcon Mamba (LLM, Technology Innovation Institute in Abu Dhabi). A powerful 7B parameter model built on the Mamba State Space Language Model (SSLM) architecture. It enables Falcon to dynamically adjust parameters and filter out irrelevant inputs, making it more efficient than transformer-based models. (Figure 2.1.15, Source: Hugging Face, 2025)
- August 13, 2024: Grok-2 (Text-to-text and text-to-image, xAI). xAI's advanced text- and image-generation model excels in image creation, advanced reasoning, and problem-solving. It rivaled leading models quickly despite xAI being founded only in March 2023. (Figure 2.1.16, Source: xAI, 2025)
- August 15, 2024: Imagen 3 (Text-to-image, Google Labs). Google's updated AI image generator achieves the highest Elo score on the GenAI-Bench image benchmark, setting a new standard for AI-generated visuals. (Figure 2.1.17, Source: Google, 2025)
- August 22, 2024: Jamba 1.5 (LLM, AI21 Labs). The first LLM to combine state-space models with transformers, delivering high-quality text-based results. This hybrid approach significantly enhances speed while preserving output quality. (Figure 2.1.18, Source: AI21, 2025)
- August 29, 2024: SynthID v2 (Tool, Google). The updated version of Google's watermarking and identification software now supports AI-generated content across images, video, audio, and text, with enhanced tracking and verification capabilities. (Figure 2.1.19, Source: Google, 2025)
- September 11, 2024: NotebookLM Podcast Tool (Text-to-podcast, Google Labs). The second end-to-end AI podcast generator to hit the market after Synthpod, it went viral among students for studying and tech employees for listening to AI-generated summaries. (Figure 2.1.20, Source: Google, 2025)
- September 12, 2024: o1-preview (Language, math, biology, OpenAI). OpenAI's first "o series" model designed for advanced reasoning and complex tasks. It is significantly more powerful than GPT, particularly in math, science, and coding. (Figure 2.1.21, Source: OpenAI, 2025)
- September 17, 2024: NVLM (D, H, X) (Vision/language, Nvidia). Nvidia's three open-access models for vision-language tasks achieved top scores on OCRBench (optical character recognition) and VQAv2 (natural language understanding). (Figure 2.1.22, Source: Dai et al., 2024)
- September 19, 2024: Qwen2.5 (LLM, Alibaba). Alibaba's latest foundation model series includes efficient smaller models and specialized coding and math models for targeted functionality. (Figure 2.1.23, Source: Qwen, 2025)
- October 16, 2024: Ministral (LLM, Mistral). A pair of compact models (3B and 8B parameters) that outperformed Gemma and Llama models of similar size across all major industry-recognized benchmarks. (Figure 2.1.24, Source: Mistral, 2025)
- October 22, 2024: Anthropic Computer Use (Agentic Capability, Anthropic). A groundbreaking computer control feature for Claude 3.5 Sonnet users that allows the model to move the cursor, type, and autonomously complete tasks on the user's computer in real time. (Figure 2.1.25, Source: Anthropic, 2025)
- October 28, 2024: Apple Intelligence (iPhone feature, Apple). A suite of AI-powered features including Image Playground, Genmoji, and Siri integration with ChatGPT. (Figure 2.1.26, Source: Apple, 2025)
- December 3, 2024: Nova Pro (Multimodal, Amazon). Amazon Web Services' most powerful model in the Nova family, capable of processing visual and textual information, with particular strength in analyzing financial documents. (Figure 2.1.27, Source: Amazon, 2025)
- December 11, 2024: Gemini 2 (LLM, Google DeepMind). The improved Gemini version includes computer control alongside image and audio generation capabilities. It is twice as fast as Gemini 1.5 Pro and offers significantly enhanced performance in coding and image analysis. (Figure 2.1.28, Source: Google, 2025)
- December 12, 2024: Sora (Text-to-video, OpenAI). A video generation model that creates videos up to 20 seconds long at 1080p for ChatGPT Pro users and five seconds at 720p for ChatGPT Plus users. Official release was delayed from early 2024 demos to improve model safety. (Figure 2.1.29, Source: OpenAI, 2025)
- December 13, 2024: Global MMLU (Dataset, Cohere). A multilingual evaluation set featuring professionally translated MMLU questions across 42 languages. It evaluates AI performance in diverse languages while addressing Western biases in the original MMLU dataset, where an estimated 28% of questions rely on Western cultural knowledge. (Figure 2.1.30, Source: Singh et al., 2025)
- December 20, 2024: o3 (beta) (Multimodal, OpenAI). OpenAI's newest frontier model, released for safety testing by AI researchers. It outperforms all previous models in SWE, competition code, competition math, PhD-level science, and research math benchmarks, and sets a new record on the ARC-AGI benchmark with 87.5% on the ARC Prize team's private holdout set. (Figure 2.1.31, Source: VentureBeat, 2025)
- December 27, 2024: DeepSeek-V3 (LLM, DeepSeek). An open-source model developed with significantly fewer computing resources than state-of-the-art models that outperforms leading models on benchmarks like MMLU and GPQA. (Figure 2.1.32, Source: Dirox, 2025)

State of AI Performance
The AI Index provides a high-level view into major AI trends that occurred in 2024. Figure 2.1.33 illustrates the progress of AI systems relative to human baselines for eight AI benchmarks corresponding to eleven tasks (such as image classification or basic-level reading comprehension). The AI Index team selected one benchmark to represent each task. This year, the AI Index team added newly released benchmarks, GPQA Diamond and MMMU, to showcase the progress of AI systems in tackling extremely challenging cognitive tasks. The chart tracks performance relative to the human baseline (%) from 2012 to 2024 across the following benchmarks: Image classification (ImageNet Top-5), Visual reasoning (VQA), Medium-level reading comprehension (SQuAD 2.0), English language understanding (SuperGLUE), Multitask language understanding (MMLU), Competition-level mathematics (MATH), PhD-level science questions (GPQA Diamond), and Multimodal understanding and reasoning (MMMU). As of 2024, there are very few task categories where human performance remains unmatched.

Note 1: An AI benchmark is a standardized test used to evaluate the performance and capabilities of AI systems on specific tasks. For example, ImageNet is a canonical AI benchmark that features a large collection of labeled images, and AI systems are tasked with classifying these images accurately. Tracking progress on benchmarks has been a standard way for the AI community to monitor the advancement of AI systems.
Note 2: In Figure 2.1.33, the values are scaled to establish a standard metric for comparing different benchmarks. The scaling function is calibrated such that the performance of the best model for each year is measured as a percentage of the human baseline for a given task. A value of 105% indicates, for example, that a model performs 5% better than the human baseline.

Perspectives on open versus closed-weight AI models are
sharply divided. Advocates of open-weight models highlight
their potential to reduce market monopolies, spur innovation,
improve security and robustness, and enhance transparency
within the AI ecosystem. For example, Meta’s Llama models
have been leveraged to create tools like Meditron, power
military applications, and drive the development of numerous
open-weight models worldwide. However, critics warn that
open-weight models pose significant security risks, including
the spread of disinformation and the creation of bioweapons,

chunk-004.context:
This section details Chapter 2 (Technical Performance), Section 2.1 (Overview of AI in 2024) from the AI Index Report 2025, focusing on the rapid narrowing of performance gaps across model openness, geography, and scale, alongside evolving benchmarking practices.

**Closed vs. Open-Weight Models**
The performance gap between AI and humans is shrinking rapidly. Even in areas where human performance previously surpassed AI, the gap between closed-weight and open-weight large language models (LLMs) is narrowing. Figure 2.1.34 illustrates this trend on the Chatbot Arena Leaderboard, a public platform for benchmarking LLM performance. In early January 2024, the leading closed-weight model outperformed the top open-weight model by 8.0%. By February 2025, this gap had narrowed to 1.7%.

On the MATH benchmark for competition-level mathematics, state-of-the-art AI systems now lead human performance by 7.9 percentage points, a significant improvement from the 0.3-point gap in 2024. On MMMU, a benchmark for complex, multidisciplinary, expert-level questions, the best 2024 model (o1) scored 78.2%, only 4.4 points below the human benchmark of 82.6%. Conversely, at the end of 2023, Google Gemini scored 59.4%, illustrating the rapid advancements in AI performance on cognitively demanding tasks. The same narrowing trend is evident across other question-answering benchmarks. In 2023, closed-weight models consistently outperformed open-weight counterparts on nearly every major benchmark: MMLU, HumanEval, MMMU, and MATH. By 2024, the gap narrowed significantly. In late 2023, closed-weight models led open models on MMLU by 15.9 points, but by the end of 2024, that difference shrank to just 0.1 percentage point. This rapid improvement was largely driven by Meta’s summer 2024 release of Llama 3.1, followed by the launch of other high-performing open-weight models such as DeepSeek’s V3.

AI models can be released with different levels of openness. Certain models, like Google’s Med-Gemini, remain entirely closed and accessible only to their developers. Meanwhile, models such as OpenAI’s GPT-4o and Anthropic’s Claude 3.5 provide limited public access through APIs. However, weights for these models are not released, preventing independent modification or thorough public scrutiny. In contrast, weights for Meta’s Llama 3.3 and Stable Video 4D are fully available, allowing anyone to modify and use them freely. Perspectives on open versus closed-weight AI models are sharply divided. Advocates of open-weight models highlight their potential to reduce market monopolies, spur innovation, improve security and robustness, and enhance transparency within the AI ecosystem. For example, Meta’s Llama models have been leveraged to create tools like Meditron, power military applications, and drive the development of numerous open-weight models worldwide. However, critics warn that open-weight models pose significant security risks, including the spread of disinformation and the creation of bioweapons, arguing for a more cautious and controlled approach.

(Note: Benchmark data was collected in early January 2025, so individual scores may have improved since publication. Regarding terminology, "open source" grants users the right to freely use, study, modify, and distribute software and source code. Open-weight models are more accessible than closed-weight models but are not necessarily fully open source, as underlying code or training data is often withheld.)

**United States vs. China Technical Performance**
The United States has historically dominated AI research and model development, with China consistently ranking second. Recent evidence suggests the landscape is rapidly changing, with China-based models catching up to their U.S. counterparts. On the LMSYS Chatbot Arena, the top U.S. model outperformed the best Chinese model by 9.3% in January 2024. By February 2025, this gap had narrowed to just 1.7%. At the end of 2023, performance gaps on benchmarks such as MMLU, MMMU, MATH, and HumanEval between U.S. and Chinese models were 17.5, 13.5, 24.3, and 31.6 percentage points, respectively. By the end of 2024, these differences had narrowed significantly to just 0.3, 8.1, 1.6, and 3.7 percentage points. The launch of DeepSeek-R1 garnered attention for another reason: the company reported achieving its results using only a fraction of the hardware resources typically required to train such a model. Beyond impacting U.S. stock markets, DeepSeek’s R1 launch raised doubts about the effectiveness of U.S. semiconductor export controls.

**Improved Performance From Smaller Models**
Recent AI progress has been driven by scaling—the idea that increasing model size and training data improves performance. While scaling has significantly boosted AI capabilities, a notable recent trend is the emergence of smaller high-performing models. Figure 2.1.38 illustrates the reduction in size of the smallest model that scores above 60% on MMLU, a widely used language model benchmark. For context, early models powering ChatGPT, such as GPT-3.5 Turbo, scored around 70% on MMLU. In 2022, the smallest model surpassing 60% on MMLU was PaLM, with 540 billion parameters. By 2024, Microsoft’s Phi-3 Mini, with just 3.8 billion parameters, achieved the same threshold, marking a 142-fold reduction in model size over two years.

2024 was a breakthrough year for smaller AI models. Nearly every major AI developer released compact, high-performing models, including GPT-4o mini, o1-mini, Gemini 2.0 Flash, Llama 3.1 8B, and Mistral Small. The rise of small models is significant for several reasons. It demonstrates increasing algorithmic efficiency, allowing developers to achieve more with less data and at lower training costs. These efficiency gains, combined with growing datasets, could lead to even higher-performing models. Additionally, inference on smaller models is typically faster and less expensive. Their emergence also lowers the barrier to entry for AI developers and businesses looking to integrate AI into their operations.

**Model Performance Convergence at the Frontier**
In recent years, AI model performance at the frontier has converged, with multiple providers now offering highly capable models. This marks a shift from late 2022, when ChatGPT’s launch—widely seen as AI’s breakthrough into public consciousness—coincided with a landscape dominated by just two major players: OpenAI and Google. OpenAI, founded in 2015, released GPT-3 in 2020, while Google introduced models like PaLM and Chinchilla in 2022. Since then, new players have entered the scene, including Meta with its Llama models, Anthropic with Claude, High-Flyer’s DeepSeek, Mistral with Le Chat, and xAI with Grok. As competition has intensified, model performance has increasingly converged. The performance gap between the highest- and 10th-ranked models on the Chatbot Arena Leaderboard fell from 11.9% to 5.4% by early 2025. Similarly, the difference between the top two models fell from 4.9% in 2023 to just 0.7% in 2024. This validates 2023 predictions that AI companies lack a technological moat to shield them from rivals.

**Benchmarking AI**
For years, the AI Index has used benchmarks to monitor the technical progress of AI systems over time. While benchmarks remain a key tool, it is important to acknowledge their limitations and guide the community toward more effective benchmarking practices. As noted in last year’s AI Index, many prominent AI benchmarks are reaching saturation. With AI systems advancing rapidly, even newly designed, more challenging tests often remain relevant for only a few years. Some experts suggest that the era of new academic benchmarks may be coming to an end. Games with a physical component or team capabilities are also good measures of progress for AI, and the robotics community has embarked on challenging game competitions such as RoboCup for soccer-playing robots. Another area where competitions are used involves coordination and teamwork, where multi-agent systems demonstrate advances in distributed reasoning.

Historically, the AI community developed benchmarks to evaluate different approaches against the same gold standard. Significant advances in AI have been possible because models with diverse data in different domains could be evaluated automatically by third parties without releasing the test data. However, when model developers release new models, they typically report benchmark scores that are often accepted at face value. This approach has flaws. In some cases, companies use nonstandard prompting techniques, making model-to-model comparisons unreliable. To truly assess the capabilities of AI systems, more rigorous and comprehensive evaluations are needed.
chunk-004.summary: The 2024 AI landscape saw rapid performance convergence: closed vs. open-weight LLM gaps on MMLU and Chatbot Arena shrank from 15.9 points and 8.0% to 0.1 percentage point and 1.7% respectively, driven by models like Llama 3.1 and DeepSeek V3. Simultaneously, U.S. vs. Chinese model gaps narrowed from 17.5-31.6 percentage points to 0.3-8.1 points, while frontier model performance differences dropped from 4.9% to 0.7%, alongside a 142-fold reduction in model size required to hit 60% on MMLU (PaLM 540B to Phi-3 Mini 3.8B).

chunk-005.context:
The AI Index tracks AI technical progress through standardized benchmarks, sourcing scores from leaderboards, public repositories like Papers With Code and RankedAGI, and official company publications. This evaluation methodology operates under the assumption that company-reported scores are accurate and factual. The benchmark scores detailed in this analysis are current as of mid-February 2025, though newer model releases since publication may have surpassed these recorded results.

Historically, AI evaluation relied on competitions designed to measure human performance or benchmark specific capabilities. However, many aspects of intelligence do not easily lend themselves to standard benchmarking. Areas such as multi-agent systems and human-AI interaction present significant challenges due to the variability of human behaviors and the diversity of correct answers. Creating high-quality, human-curated benchmarks is also expensive and time-consuming. The rapid progress of AI systems is perhaps best illustrated by the diminishing relevance of the Turing test. Originally proposed in Alan Turing’s 1950 paper "Computing Machinery and Intelligence," the test evaluates a machine’s ability to exhibit humanlike intelligence through a text-based conversation where a human judge cannot reliably distinguish the machine from a human. Recent evidence indicates that large language models have advanced so significantly that humans now struggle to differentiate the best-performing models from actual humans, suggesting modern AI can pass the test.

A major advancement in AI is the integration of previously separate intelligent capabilities into single systems. Natural language processing was historically addressed as a collection of separate tasks—such as reading comprehension, logical reasoning, text generation, and question answering—each with dedicated models and benchmarks. Speech tasks were also benchmarked separately from language understanding or generation tasks. Today, a single model can address all language tasks, and in some cases, a single model can simultaneously address language, images, and multimodal tasks. This convergence is a critical advance for capability integration. In robotics, benchmarks evaluate physical world interaction and natural law reasoning. Examples include ARMBench, which focuses on perception tasks, and VIMA-Bench, which assesses robot performance in simulated environments where models simultaneously integrate perception, communication, and deep learning.

The Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) benchmark, created in 2020 by researchers from UC Berkeley, Columbia University, the University of Chicago, and the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, serves as a premier evaluation tool. MMLU assesses model performance in zero-shot or few-shot scenarios across 57 subjects spanning the humanities, STEM, and social sciences. The established human baseline for MMLU is 89.8%. On September 2024, OpenAI’s o1-preview model achieved the highest recorded score of 92.3%. For comparison, GPT-4, launched in March 2023, scored 86.4% on the same benchmark, while the earlier model RoBERTa achieved just 27.9% in 2019. This progression represents a 64.4 percentage point increase in state-of-the-art performance over five years. 

Despite its prominence, MMLU has faced notable criticisms, including claims that the benchmark contains erroneous or overly simplistic questions that fail to challenge increasingly advanced systems. In 2024, researchers from the University of Toronto, the University of Waterloo, and Carnegie Mellon University introduced MMLU-Pro, a more rigorous variant designed to eliminate noisy and trivial questions, expand complex ones, and increase the number of available answer choices for models. DeepSeek-R1 posted the highest score to date on MMLU-Pro at 84.0%.

Evaluating public preference for AI models is tracked via the Chatbot Arena Leaderboard, launched in 2023 by LMSYS. The platform allows users to query two anonymous models and vote for the preferred text generation. By early 2025, the platform accumulated over one million votes, with users ranking one of Google’s Gemini models as the community’s most preferred choice. The performance gap between the top-ranked and 10th-ranked models on the leaderboard has narrowed significantly, falling from 11.9% in 2023 to 5.4% by early 2025, highlighting growing parity in recent large language model quality.

Benchmark reliability faces challenges from contamination, where large language models encounter test questions present in their original training data. A recent study by Scale documented significant contamination in the performance of many large language models on GSM8K, a widely used mathematics benchmark. Researchers have sought to combat this issue by introducing benchmarks like LiveBench, which are periodically updated with new questions from unfamiliar sources that language models are unlikely to have encountered during training. Furthermore, developers sometimes report benchmark scores using non-standard prompting techniques that artificially boost performance but hinder accurate model-to-model comparisons. For example, when Google launched Gemini Ultra, the company reported an MMLU benchmark score using a chain-of-thought prompting technique that other developers did not use. Evidence shows that developer-reported scores can differ by as much as five percentage points from those later evaluated by independent academic researchers. To address systemic quality issues, the BetterBench research team systematically analyzed 24 prominent benchmarks and identified critical deficiencies: 14 benchmarks failed to report statistical significance, 17 lacked scripts for result replication, and most suffered from inadequate documentation. In response, the researchers proposed a 46-criteria framework covering the entire benchmark lifecycle and introduced a publicly accessible repository to enable continuous updates and improve benchmark comparability.
chunk-005.summary: The AI Index tracks AI progress using benchmarks current as of mid-February 2025, documenting a 64.4 percentage point increase in MMLU scores from RoBERTa's 27.9% in 2019 to OpenAI's o1-preview 92.3% in September 2024, alongside a narrowed Chatbot Arena performance gap from 11.9% to 5.4% by early 2025. To combat benchmark contamination and reporting inconsistencies, the research community introduced MMLU-Pro, LiveBench, and a comprehensive 46-criteria evaluation framework.

chunk-006.context:
The AI Index Report 2025 outlines advanced evaluation frameworks and frontier model releases focused on language understanding and automated reasoning. BenchBuilder, developed by UC Berkeley researchers, leverages large language models to automate the curation of high-quality, open-ended prompts from crowdsourced datasets, enabling benchmark creation or updates with minimal human involvement. The LMSYS team utilized this pipeline to build Arena-Hard-Auto, a benchmark for evaluating instruction-tuned large language models. Arena-Hard-Auto incorporates 500 challenging user queries extracted from Chatbot Arena and employs GPT-4 Turbo as the judge to compare model outputs against the baseline GPT-4-0314. To account for how response formatting influences user preference, the framework includes a style control leaderboard. The benchmark faces criticism for uneven question distribution, with over 50 percent of prompts focusing exclusively on coding and debugging. As of November 2024, the highest-scoring models on Arena-Hard-Auto were o1-mini (92.0), o1-preview (90.4), and Claude-3.5-Sonnet (85.2). Model rankings on the style control leaderboard included claude-3-5-sonnet-2024-10-22, gpt-4-turbo-2024-04-09, yi-lightning, athene-v2-chat, and llama-3.1-nemotron-70b-instruct.

To address evaluation limitations, the Allen Institute for AI and the University of Washington launched WildBench in 2024. This framework targets challenging real-world queries, noting that older metrics like MMLU prioritize academic questions over practical problems, while platforms like LMSYS rely heavily on inconsistent human oversight. WildBench provides an automated evaluation pipeline populated with real-world questions meticulously selected from over one million human-chatbot interactions. The benchmark's question bank is periodically updated, and its live leaderboard ranks GPT-4o at the top with an Elo score of 1227.1, narrowly ahead of second-place Claude 3.5 Sonnet at 1215.4.

OpenAI's o1 and o3 models demonstrate a paradigm shift in automated reasoning through inference-time compute, commonly referred to as test-time computation. These models utilize chain-of-thought processing and iterative answer-checking to break complex problems into manageable steps before execution, significantly enhancing output quality in programming, quantum physics, logic, and text decryption. When compared to GPT-4o, o1 achieves a 2.8-point improvement on MMLU, a 34.5-point gain on MATH, a 26.7-point increase on GPQA Diamond, and a 65.1-point lead on AIME 2024. The o3 model demonstrates superior complex reasoning, achieving an 87.5 percent accuracy rate on the ARC-AGI machine intelligence benchmark, surpassing the previous record of 55.5 percent. Despite these capabilities, the models carry higher financial and latency costs: GPT-4o costs $2.50 per one million input tokens and $10 per one million output tokens, whereas o1 costs $15 per one million input tokens and $60 per one million output tokens. Additionally, o1 processes inputs approximately 40 times slower than GPT-4o, taking 29.7 seconds to produce the first token compared to GPT-4o's 0.72 seconds. OpenAI initially released o1-preview to ChatGPT Plus and Teams users on September 12, 2024, and fully launched o1 alongside ChatGPT Pro access on December 5, 2024. The o3 model remains restricted to select researchers and developers through OpenAI's safety testing program.

Another newly released evaluation framework, MixEval, was developed by researchers at the National University of Singapore, Carnegie Mellon University, and the Allen Institute for AI to address current evaluation shortcomings. MixEval merges comprehensive, well-distributed real-world queries similar to Chatbot Arena with ground-truth-based questions found in MMLU. Its MixEval-Hard suite focuses on substantially more difficult prompts. The highest-scoring model on MixEval-Hard is OpenAI's o1-preview with a score of 72.0, followed by Claude 3.5 Sonnet-0620 and third-place Llama-3.1-405B-Instruct, which scored 66.2; all three models were released in 2024.

The report also examines Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), a capability that integrates large language models with document retrieval mechanisms to tailor responses to user queries based on retrieved information, with applications ranging from database Q&A to customer support. In September 2024, Anthropic introduced Contextual Retrieval to improve RAG efficiency. The year 2024 also saw the launch of specialized RAG benchmarks including Ragnarok, CRAG, and FinanceBench. Concurrently, the Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard evaluates the ability of large language models to accurately invoke functions or tools. Its evaluation suite contains over 2,000 question-function-answer pairs spanning Python, Java, JavaScript, and REST APIs across multiple domains. The top-performing model on this leaderboard is watt-tool-70b, a function-calling-optimized fine-tuned variant of Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, which achieved an overall accuracy of 74.31. A November variant of GPT-4o ranked second with a score of 72.08. Performance on this benchmark demonstrated substantial improvement throughout 2024, with top models at the year's end achieving accuracies up to 50 percentage points higher than those recorded early in the year.
chunk-006.summary: The AI Index Report 2025 details advanced evaluation frameworks like BenchBuilder, WildBench, and MixEval alongside specialized benchmarks for retrieval-augmented generation and function calling. It documents OpenAI's o1 and o3 models, which demonstrate advanced reasoning through test-time computation but carry higher costs and latency than GPT-4o, alongside significant performance gains across multiple leaderboards reaching up to 87.5% accuracy on ARC-AGI.

chunk-007.context:
The Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB), developed by a team at Hugging Face and Cohere and introduced in late 2022, comprehensively evaluates how models perform on embedding tasks. Embedding converts data, such as words, texts, or documents, into numerical vectors that capture semantic meanings and distances between vectors. This transformation process is essential for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), as it enables models to search for relevant information after transforming user queries into embedding vectors. The MTEB includes 58 datasets spanning 112 languages and eight embedding tasks: bitext mining, classification, clustering, pair classification, reranking, retrieval, semantic textual similarity, and summarization. In bitext mining, the model matches sentences across two different languages. As of early 2025, Voyage AI’s voyage-3-m-exp leads the MTEB leaderboard with a score of 74.03. Voyage AI specializes in creating high-quality AI embedding models. The voyage-3-m-exp model is a variant of the voyage-3-large foundation model designed specifically for embedding tasks, and it utilizes strategies like Matryoshka Representation Learning and quantization-aware training. This model narrowly outperformed NV-Embed-v2, which scored 72.31 and held the top position for most of 2024. When the MTEB benchmark launched in late 2022, the leading model achieved an average score of 59.5, demonstrating meaningful performance improvements over the subsequent two years.

As large language models expanded their context windows from 4,000 to 8,000 tokens (as seen with 2023 models like GPT-4 and Llama 2) to 128,000 to 2 million tokens (as seen with May 2024 models like GPT-4o and Gemini 2.0 Pro Experimental), evaluating their performance in long-context settings became increasingly critical. Existing evaluations previously relied on limited needle-in-the-haystack scenarios that only provided baseline assessments. To address this limitation, Nvidia introduced the RULER benchmark in 2024 to assess long-context performance through retrieval, multihop reasoning, aggregation, and question answering. According to February 2025 results, Gemini-1.5-Pro achieved the highest weighted performance average of 95.5 on RULER, followed by GPT-4 at 89.0 and GLM4 at 88.0. The RULER researchers discovered that many models claiming context sizes of 32,000 tokens or greater fail to maintain satisfactory performance at that length, revealing that their actual operational context windows are shorter than advertised. Additionally, HELMET, a long-context evaluation benchmark introduced in 2024 through a collaboration between Intel and Princeton University, targets the inadequacies of prior benchmarks, including insufficient downstream task coverage, short context lengths, and unreliable metrics. HELMET features seven long-context evaluation categories and tests models across 8,000, 32,000, and 128,000 context settings. On the HELMET benchmark, models including GPT-4, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and Llama 3.1-70B experience performance degradation in longer context settings, while Gemini 1.5 Pro and the August variant of GPT-4 maintain their effectiveness.

In image and video understanding, computer vision allows machines to comprehend and create visuals. While early deep learning relied on ImageNet for image understanding, modern benchmarks test more complex reasoning. The Visual Commonsense Reasoning (VCR) challenge, introduced in 2019 by researchers from the University of Washington and the Allen Institute for AI, tests AI systems' commonsense visual reasoning abilities by requiring them to answer questions based on images and reason about the logic behind those answers. Performance is measured using the Q->AR score, which evaluates both question answering and rationale selection. The human baseline for VCR is a score of 85.0. In July 2024, a model posted to the VCR leaderboard achieved a score of 85.0, matching the human baseline and marking a 4.2% improvement since 2023. Another benchmark, MVBench, was introduced in late 2023 by researchers from the Chinese Academy of Sciences, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Shanghai AI Laboratory, University of Hong Kong, Fudan University, and Nanjing University. MVBench tests multimodal video understanding and temporal reasoning across multiple frames, unlike earlier benchmarks that focused on spatial understanding through static images. As of 2024, the top MVBench model is Video-CCAM-7B-v1.2, built on the Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct language model, which achieved a score of 69.23. This score represents a 14.6% improvement on the benchmark since its late 2023 introduction. Regarding image generation, current AI generators are so advanced that most people struggle to differentiate between AI-generated images and actual images of human faces.

chunk-008.context:
This section details progress in image generation, video synthesis, speech recognition, and automated coding benchmarks. Midjourney’s image generation models from 2022 to 2025 demonstrate significant improvements in hyper-realism using the prompt “a hyper-realistic image of Harry Potter.” In 2022, early versions (V1 through V4) produced cartoonish and inaccurate renderings, but by 2025, later versions (V6.1) generate startlingly realistic depictions. This evolution occurred alongside the growth of the Chatbot Arena Vision leaderboard, which ranks over 50 vision models based on user-submitted text-to-image prompts like “Batman drinking a coffee.” By early 2025, Google’s Gemini-2.0-Flash-Thinking-Exp-1219 leads the Vision Arena with more than 150,000 user votes. The performance gap between the top model and the fourth-ranked model, ChatGPT-4o-latest (released November 20, 2024), is only 3.4%.

The AI industry experienced rapid advances in text-to-video generation in 2024, building on earlier models that struggled with low quality, lack of sound, and short clip lengths. In November 2023, Stability AI launched Stable Video Diffusion, its first foundation model for high-quality video generation. Stability AI subsequently released Stable Video 3D in March 2024 to generate 3D views and videos from single images. In March 2024, OpenAI previewed Sora, a diffusion-based video generation model that creates 20-second clips at up to 1080p resolution by progressively refining a base video; it became publicly accessible in December 2024. Meta introduced its advanced Movie Gen model in October 2024, which supports instruction-based video editing, sound incorporation, and 16-second 1080p videos at 16 frames per second. Google launched Veo in May 2024 and Veo 2 in December 2024; internal benchmarks show Veo 2 consistently outperformed Movie Gen, Kling v1.5, and Sora Turbo in user preference tests. Other contributors include Runway’s Gen-3 Alpha, Luma’s Dream Machine, and Kuaishou’s Kling 1.5. The trajectory of improvement is visible in Pika’s generations of the prompt “Will Smith eating spaghetti,” which showed dramatic quality gains between versions released in December 2023 (V1.0) and February 2025 (V2.2).

AI speech recognition has matured to the point where transcription is highly reliable for dictation applications. The LRS2 (Lip Reading Sentences 2) dataset, introduced in 2017, remains a standard for evaluating lip-reading and automatic speech recognition (ASR) using the word error rate (WER) metric, where lower scores indicate higher accuracy. In 2024, the model Whisper-Flamingo achieved a new state-of-the-art WER of 1.3% on the LRS2 benchmark, surpassing the previous record of 1.5% set in 2023. Because the error rate is already extremely low, significant future improvements appear unlikely, suggesting the benchmark is nearing saturation.

Large language models have become highly proficient at coding, leading to benchmark saturation and the creation of more complex evaluation suites. HumanEval, introduced by OpenAI in 2021, tests coding ability through 164 handwritten programming problems. In early 2025, Claude 3.5 Sonnet (HPT) achieved a perfect 100% Pass@1 score on this benchmark. SWE-bench, launched in October 2023 by researchers from Princeton and the University of Chicago, evaluates software engineering skills using 2,294 real-world GitHub issues and Python repository problems. It features a Lite subset for accessibility and a Verified subset filtered by human annotators. On the SWE-bench Verified set, performance jumped from 4.4% at the end of 2023 to 71.7% for OpenAI’s o3 model in early 2025. To address limitations in testing multi-function invocations and natural-language coding instructions, an international team released BigCodeBench in 2024. This comprehensive benchmark requires LLMs to invoke functions across 139 libraries and 7 domains across 1,140 fine-grained tasks. OpenAI’s o1 model achieved an average Pass@1 score of 35.5 on BigCodeBench’s hard subset. Additionally, the Chatbot Arena Coding filter tracks community perception of model coding skills. As of early 2025, Gemini-Exp-1206 leads the coding arena with an Elo score of 1,369, followed closely by OpenAI’s o1 at 1,361, and Chinese model DeepSeek-V3 at 1,317, representing a 3.8% gap between first and third place.
chunk-008.summary: As of early 2025, AI systems have achieved near-human or superior performance across major technical benchmarks, with Claude 3.5 Sonnet scoring 100% on HumanEval, OpenAI’s o3 solving 71.7% of SWE-bench Verified tasks, and Whisper-Flamingo achieving a 1.3% word error rate on LRS2. Concurrently, video and image generation models like Sora, Veo 2, and Midjourney V6.1 have dramatically improved in realism and fidelity, while community preference gaps on Chatbot Arena have narrowed to under 4% across vision and coding categories.

chunk-009.context:
The AI Index Report 2025 Chapter 2 evaluates technical performance through standardized benchmarks focusing on mathematical reasoning and general AI capabilities.

**Mathematics Evaluation**
GSM8K, introduced by OpenAI in 2021, contains approximately 8,000 grade-school math word problems and challenges AI models to generate multistep solutions using arithmetic operations. Alongside MMLU, it is a widely used benchmark for evaluating advanced large language models, though concerns regarding potential contamination and benchmark saturation have emerged. The top-performing model on GSM8K is a variant of Claude Sonnet 3.5 optimized using the HPT prompting strategy, which achieved a 97.72% accuracy score. This represents a significant improvement over the previous high of 91.00% in 2023. However, in 2024, multiple models from Mistral, Meta, and Qwen scored around 96%, indicating that the GSM8K benchmark may be approaching saturation.

The MATH dataset, introduced in 2021 by researchers from UC Berkeley and the University of Chicago, contains 12,500 challenging, competition-level mathematics problems. AI systems initially solved only 6.9% of these problems when the benchmark was first released. Performance improved dramatically, and in January 2025, OpenAI’s o3-mini (high) model solved 97.9% of the problems, surpassing the 90% human baseline for the first time.

The LMSYS Chatbot Arena includes a dedicated math filter that evaluates over 181 models based on public preference for math-related answers, accumulating more than 340,000 public votes. Unlike the coding arena where Gemini-based models lead, the top-ranked model in the Math Arena is OpenAI’s o1 variant, which was released in December 2024.

To address the saturation of high school and college-level benchmarks like GSM8K and MATH, Epoch AI introduced FrontierMath. This benchmark features hundreds of original, exceptionally challenging problems vetted by expert mathematicians, often requiring hours, days, or collaborative research efforts to solve. The problems test advanced mathematics including number theory, real analysis, algebraic geometry, and category theory. When evaluated on FrontierMath, Gemini 1.5 Pro achieved the highest score of 2.0% among six leading LLMs (o1-preview, o1-mini, GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Grok 2 Beta, and Gemini 1.5 Pro 002). OpenAI’s o3 model scored 25.2% on the benchmark.

**Theorem Proving and Mathematical Systems**
DeepMind developed AlphaProof, a reinforcement learning system derived from AlphaZero, to solve mathematical problems by generating hypotheses that are verified using the Lean interactive proof system. A fine-tuned Gemini model translates natural language problem statements into formal representations to build a comprehensive training library. AlphaGeometry 2 is a neuro-symbolic hybrid system featuring a language model based on Gemini and trained on extensive synthetic data. Prior to 2024, AlphaGeometry solved 83% of historical International Mathematical Olympiad (IMO) geometry problems. The IMO, established in 1959, is the world’s oldest and most prestigious competition for young mathematicians. During the 2024 competition, AlphaGeometry solved the sole geometry problem in just 24 seconds, while AlphaProof solved 25 out of 30 Olympiad geometry problems, surpassing the average score of an IMO silver medalist (22.9). AlphaProof also successfully solved two algebra problems and one number theory problem but failed to solve two combinatorics problems.

Automatic theorem-proving systems are also evaluated on the TPTP benchmark, which has been used since 1997 to assess performance on software verification and logic problems. A 2024 update of TPTP v.9.0.0, containing over 25,000 problems, indicates that fully automatic systems can now solve 89% of its problems. Cross-testing these systems remains unfeasible due to differing logical frameworks and a lack of translators between them, while the TPTP library size is insufficient to serve as a training set for AlphaProof without generating substantial synthetic examples.

**General Reasoning Benchmarks**
General reasoning evaluates AI systems' ability to draw logically valid conclusions across broad, multidisciplinary domains rather than narrow tasks. The MMMU benchmark, developed by researchers from the United States and Canada, assesses this using approximately 11,500 college-level questions across six core disciplines: art and design, business, science, health and medicine, humanities and social science, and technology and engineering. Questions utilize formats including charts, maps, tables, and chemical structures. As of January 2025, OpenAI’s o1 model achieved a 78.2% score on MMMU, a significant improvement from the 59.4% state-of-the-art score reported in the previous year. This score remains below the 82.6% medium human expert baseline, though AI systems are rapidly closing the gap.

The GPQA benchmark, introduced in 2023 by researchers from NYU, Anthropic, and Meta, tests graduate-level general and multisubject reasoning using 448 difficult multiple-choice questions crafted by subject-matter experts in biology, physics, and chemistry. These questions cannot be answered by web search. On the dataset's most challenging "diamond" subset, human experts achieved an 81.3% accuracy rate. OpenAI’s o3 model, launched in December 2024, scored 87.7%, exceeding the human expert baseline and marking a 48.9 percentage point improvement over 2023's state-of-the-art.

The ARC-AGI benchmark addresses claims regarding artificial general intelligence by testing a system's ability to generalize beyond prior training. It presents AI systems with a set of independent tasks, each containing demonstration or input pairs followed by test or output scenarios, rather than relying on memorization or narrow pattern matching.
chunk-009.summary: The AI Index Report 2025 details how AI systems are rapidly surpassing human baselines on mathematical benchmarks like MATH (97.9% accuracy with OpenAI's o3-mini) and GPQA (87.7% accuracy, exceeding the 81.3% expert baseline), while advanced reasoning tests like MMMU (78.2%) and FrontierMath continue to push model capabilities into highly complex, graduate-level domains.

chunk-010.context:
The AI Index Report 2025 details advanced evaluation benchmarks focused on generalized learning, automated reasoning, and AI agency. To properly assess AI capabilities, researchers emphasize that evaluation must encompass the capacity for general learning and skill acquisition, describing artificial general intelligence as a system 'capable of efficiently acquiring new skills and solving novel problems for which it was neither designed nor trained.'

**ARC-AGI Benchmark**
ARC-AGI is a benchmark introduced in 2019 by François Chollet, the creator of the Keras deep-learning framework, to measure generalized learning. It is impossible for systems to prepare in advance for this benchmark because each task introduces a unique logic. The tasks require no specialized world knowledge or language skills but instead draw on assumed prior knowledge, such as the concept of objects, basic topology, and elementary arithmetic—concepts typically mastered by children at an early age. When first run in 2020, the top-performing system on ARC-AGI achieved a score of only 20%. Four years later, in 2024, this score had risen to just 33%. In 2025, OpenAI’s o3 model achieved a score of 75.7%. When o3 was allocated a high-compute budget exceeding the benchmark’s $10,000 limit, it achieved a score of 87.5% on ARC-AGI-1 using the private evaluation set.

**Humanity’s Last Exam (HLE)**
As many popular AI benchmarks reach saturation, researchers behind the MMLU benchmark recently introduced Humanity’s Last Exam (HLE), a new benchmark comprising 2,700 highly challenging questions across dozens of subject areas. The dataset features multimodal questions contributed by subject matter experts, including leading professors and graduate-level reviewers, that resist simple internet lookups or database retrieval. Each question was tested against state-of-the-art LLMs before inclusion; if an existing model could answer it, the question was rejected. Initial testing indicates that HLE remains highly challenging for current AI systems. Even top models, such as OpenAI’s o1, score just 8.8%. Accuracy scores on the benchmark are as follows: GPT-4o achieved 3.10%, Grok-2 achieved 3.90%, Claude 3.5 Sonnet achieved 4.80%, Gemini 1.5 Pro achieved 5.20%, Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking achieved 7.20%, and o1 achieved 8.80%. Researchers behind HLE are closely monitoring how quickly LLMs improve, and they speculate that performance could exceed 50% by the end of 2025.

**Planning and PlanBench**
Planning is an intelligent task that involves reasoning about actions that alter the world, requiring consideration of hypothetical future states, including potential external actions and other transformative events. A group from Arizona State University proposed PlanBench, a benchmark suite containing problems used in the automated planning community, especially those used in the International Planning Competition. PlanBench tests models on 600 problems in which a hand tries to construct stacks of blocks when it is only allowed to move one block at a time to a table or to the top of a clear block. Released in 2022, the benchmark initially demonstrated that models like GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 struggled with planning tasks. OpenAI’s o1 showed significant improvements on PlanBench, though it still struggles with reliable and consistent planning. In the Blocksworld zero-shot evaluation domain, o1 achieved a score of 97.8%, far surpassing the next best LLM, Llama 3.1 405B (62.6%), and dramatically outperforming GPT-4o (35.5%). In the more challenging Mystery Blocksworld domain, where some answers are syntactically obfuscated, o1 scored 52.8% zero-shot, compared to just 0.8% for Llama 3.1 405B and 0.0% for GPT-4. Planning is a combinatorial problem, and solving problems with long solutions is expected to take more than linear time. Not surprisingly, when tested on instances that require at least 20 steps, o1 manages to solve just 23.6%. The release of OpenAI’s o1 was met with enthusiasm from the AI research community, as it was designed to actively reason rather than function purely as an autoregressive large language model.

**AI Agents and VisualAgentBench**
AI agents, which are autonomous or semiautonomous systems designed to operate within specific environments to accomplish goals, represent a significant frontier in AI research with applications ranging from academic research assistance and meeting scheduling to online shopping and vacation booking. For decades, the topic has been widely discussed in the AI community, yet few benchmarks have achieved widespread adoption, including AgentBench and MLAgentBench featured in previous years. This lag stems from the inherent complexity of benchmarking agentic tasks, which are typically more diverse, dynamic, and variable than tasks like image classification or answering language questions. VisualAgentBench (VAB), launched in 2024, represents a significant step forward by reflecting the growing multimodality of AI models and their proficiency in navigating virtual and embodied environments. VAB tests agents across three broad categories: embodied agents (operating in household and gaming environments), GUI agents (interacting with mobile and web applications), and visual design agents (such as CSS debugging). VAB presents a significant challenge for AI systems. The top-performing model, GPT-4o, achieves an overall success rate of just 36.2%. Other models' success rates on the VAB test set are as follows: GPT-4o-turbo achieved 29.90%, Gemini-1.5-Pro achieved 31.70%, Claude-3.5-Sonnet achieved 26.90%, GPT-4-02 achieved 20.50%, Llama-3.3-70B achieved 21.90%, GPT-4o-mini achieved 19.80%, o1-preview achieved 16.00%, GPT-4-turbo achieved 12.00%, Gemini-2.0-Flash achieved 10.50%, GPT-4 achieved 10.30%, Claude-3.5-Instant achieved 8.90%, GPT-4-01 achieved 8.40%, Llama-3.1-8B achieved 7.70%, and o1-mini achieved 6.30%. Most proprietary language models average around 20%. According to the benchmark’s authors, these results reveal that current AI models are far from ready for direct deployment in agentic settings.

**RE-Bench**
The emergence of increasingly capable agentic AI systems has fueled predictions that AI might soon take on the work of computer scientists or researchers. Until 2024, few benchmarks rigorously tested the R&D capabilities of top-performing AI systems. That year, researchers launched RE-Bench, featuring seven challenging, open-ended machine learning research environments. These tasks were informed by data from 71 eight-hour attempts by over 60 human experts, including optimizing a kernel, conducting a scaling law experiment, and fine-tuning GPT-2 for question answering. Researchers comparing humans and frontier AI models found that in short time-horizon settings, such as with a two-hour budget, the best AI systems achieve scores four times higher than human experts. However, as the time budget increases, human performance begins to surpass that of AI. With an eight-hour budget, human performance slightly exceeds AI, and with a 32-hour budget, humans outperform AI by a factor of two. The researchers also note that for certain tasks, AI agents already demonstrate expertise comparable to humans but can deliver results significantly faster and at a lower cost. For example, AI agents can write custom Triton kernels more quickly than any human expert.

**GAIA Benchmark**
GAIA is a benchmark for General AI assistants introduced by Meta in May 2024. It consists of 466 questions designed to assess AI systems’ ability to perform a broad range of tasks, including reasoning, multimodal processing, web browsing, and tool use. Unlike straightforward, exam-style questions, GAIA challenges AI models with complex, multistep problems that may require searching the open web, interpreting multimodal inputs, and reasoning through intricate scenarios. When researchers launched GAIA, they found that existing LLMs lagged significantly behind human performance. For instance, GPT-4 with plugins correctly answered only 15% of the questions, compared to 92% for human respondents. Performance on GAIA has improved rapidly. chunk-011.context:
The AI Index Report 2025 Chapter 2 section 2.9, titled "Robotics and Autonomous Motion," examines advancements in the field driven by the rise of foundation models, which enable robots to iteratively learn from their surroundings, adapt flexibly to new environments, and make autonomous decisions. This section details key robotic benchmarks, humanoid robot developments, DeepMind's algorithmic contributions, the emergence of robotic foundation models, and the current state of self-driving cars.

**Robotics RLBench Benchmark**
One of the most widely adopted benchmarks in the robotics community is the RLBench (Robot Learning Benchmark), launched in 2019. RLBench features 100 unique tasks of varying complexity, ranging from simple target reaching (the process by which a robotic system moves its end-effector toward a specific goal position or object in space) to opening an oven and placing a tray inside. Researchers typically evaluate new robotic systems on a standardized subset of 18 tasks to gauge performance. As of January 2025, the top-performing model on this subset is SAM2Act, a collaboration between researchers at the University of Washington, Universidad Católica San Pablo, Nvidia, and the Allen Institute for AI. SAM2Act achieved a 86.8% success rate, marking a 2.8 percentage point improvement over the previous state-of-the-art in 2024 and a 66.7 percentage point increase from the leading score in 2021.

**Highlight: Humanoid Robotics**
The year 2024 was significant for the growing prevalence of humanoid robots—machines with humanlike bodies designed to mimic human functions. For example, Figure AI, a robotics startup dedicated to developing general-purpose humanoid robots, launched its most advanced model, the Figure 02, in 2024. The Figure 02 stands 5 feet 6 inches tall, weighs 154 pounds, can handle a 44-pound payload, and operates for up to five hours on a single charge. Figure robots are able to perform complex tasks such as making coffee and assisting in automotive assembly by placing sheet metal into a car fixture. They are also integrated with OpenAI to engage in speech-to-speech reasoning, whereby the robot explains its actions and responds to queries about its behavior. Figure's success follows that of other companies that released humanoid robots, like Tesla’s Optimus (first launched in 2002 and redesigned in 2023) and Boston Dynamics’ Atlas humanoid.

**Highlight: DeepMind’s Developments**
In 2023, DeepMind launched two robotic models, PaLM-E and RT-2. These models were novel in their use of transformer-based architectures, typically found in language modeling, and their training on both manipulation data and language data. This dual training approach enabled them to excel at both robotic manipulation and text generation. In 2024, DeepMind introduced AutoRT, an AI system that leverages large foundation models to autonomously generate diverse training data for robots. AutoRT coordinates multiple video-equipped robots, guides them through various environments, devises creative tasks for them to perform, and meticulously documents these tasks. This documentation then serves as training data for future robotic learning. To date, AutoRT has generated a dataset of 77,000 robotic trials spanning 6,650 unique tasks. Greater amounts of robotic training data are important to improve the training of future robotic systems.

Conversely, SARA-RT, also from Google DeepMind, improves the efficiency of transformer-based robotic models by significantly increasing their speed. While transformers are powerful, they are also computationally intensive because they rely on quadratic complexity attention mechanisms. This means that doubling the input size of data provided to a model can quadruple computational requirements. This computational limitation complicates attempts to scale robotic models. SARA-RT addresses this challenge with a technique called "up-training," which converts the quadratic complexity of standard transformers into a linear model. This method drastically reduces computational demands while maintaining performance quality. In point cloud processing, which enables robots to interpret 3D environments, and in image processing, SARA-based models run significantly faster while avoiding major increases in run-time at scale. The researchers demonstrated that combining a large imitation learning dataset with a transformer-based learning architecture is a highly effective approach for overcoming these difficulties. The ALOHA (Autonomous Learning of High-level Activities) approach and DemoStart enabled robots to effectively learn a diverse range of tasks, including hanging a shirt, stacking kitchen items, and tying shoelaces. ALOHA-trained robots achieved high success rates across specific tasks including shirt hanging, shoelace tying, robot finger replacement, gear insertion (GearInsert-1, GearInsert-2, GearInsert-3), and various random kitchen stacking combinations (RandomKitchen-Bowl, RandomKitchen-Bowl+Cup, RandomKitchen-Bowl+Cup+Fork, LaceEasy, LaceMessy, ShirtEasy, ShirtMessy).

Similarly, DemoStart introduces a novel auto-curriculum reinforcement learning method that enables a robotic arm to master complex behaviors using only sparse rewards and a limited number of demonstrations. DeepMind also introduced a robotic model in 2024 that was capable of reaching amateur human-level performance in competitive table tennis. Given that achieving human-level speed and performance on real-world tasks is an important benchmark for robotics research, this achievement represents a notable step forward in robotic ability.

**Highlight: Foundation Models for Robotics**
In 2024, the industry pushed strongly toward developing foundational models for robotics—systems capable of reasoning with language while physically operating in the real world. Nvidia introduced GR00T (Generalist Robot 00 Technology), a general-purpose foundation model for humanoid robots designed to understand natural language and mimic human movements. Alongside GR00T, Nvidia released data pipelines, simulation frameworks, and the Thor robotics computer. This robotic development suite is intended to make it easier for the robotic community to scale and build increasingly advanced robotics. Nvidia was not alone in this space. Covariant launched RFM-1, a robotic foundation model with language capabilities and real-world maneuverability. Meanwhile, LLaRA, developed by researchers at Stony Brook University and the University of Wisconsin-Madison, integrates perception, communication, and action into a monolithic, end-to-end deep learning model. These new models continue a trend from 2023, which saw the launch of robotic foundation models like RT-2, PaLM-E, and Open-X Embodiment.

**Self-Driving Cars**
Self-driving vehicles have long been a goal for AI researchers and technologists, though their widespread adoption has been slower than anticipated. Despite predictions that fully autonomous driving is imminent, widespread use has yet to become a reality. In cities like San Francisco and Phoenix, fleets of self-driving taxis are now operating commercially. Cruise, a subsidiary of General Motors, launched its autonomous vehicles in San Francisco in late 2022 before having its license suspended in 2023 after a litany of safety incidents. Waymo, a subsidiary of Alphabet, began deploying its robotaxis in Phoenix in early 2022 and expanded to San Francisco in 2024. Waymo has since emerged as one of the more successful players in the self-driving industry. As of January 2025, Waymo operates in four major U.S. cities: Phoenix, San Francisco, Los Angeles, and Austin. Data sourced from October 2024 suggests that across these four cities, the company provides 150,000 paid rides per week, covering over a million miles. The specific rider-only miles driven without a human driver through September 2024 were: Los Angeles (1.947 million), San Francisco (10.209 million), Phoenix (20.823 million), and Austin (124,000). Looking ahead, Waymo plans to test its vehicles in 10 additional cities, including Las Vegas, San Diego, and Miami. The company chose testing locations, such as upstate New York and Truckee, California, that experience snowy weather so it can assess the vehicles in diverse driving conditions.

China’s self-driving revolution is also accelerating, led by companies like Baidu’s Apollo Go, which reported 988,000 rides across China in Q3 2024, reflecting a 20% year-over-year increase. In October 2024, the company was operating 400 robotaxis and announced plans to expand its fleet to 1,000 by the end of 2025. Pony.AI, another Chinese autonomous vehicle manufacturer, has pledged to scale its robotaxi fleet from 200 to at least 1,000 vehicles, with expectations that the fleet will reach 2,000 to 3,000 by the end of 2026. China is leading the way in autonomous vehicle testing, with reports indicating that it is testing more driverless cars than any other country and currently rolling them out across 16 cities. Robotaxis in China are notably affordable, even cheaper than rides provided by human drivers in some cases. To support this growth, China has prioritized establishing national regulations to govern the deployment of driverless cars. Beyond the self-driving revolution taking place in the U.S. and China, European startups like Wayve are beginning to gain traction in the industry.

Progress in self-driving trucks also continues, with companies like Kodiak completing its first driverless deliveries and Aurora reporting steady advancements, including over 1 million miles of autonomous freight hauling on U.S. highways since 2021, albeit with human safety drivers present. Challenges remain in bringing this technology to market, with Aurora recently announcing it would delay the commercial launch of its fleet from the end of 2024 until April 2025.

**Technical Innovations and New Benchmarks**
Over the past year, self-driving technology has advanced significantly in both vehicle capabilities and benchmarking methods. In October 2024, Tesla unveiled the Cybercab, a two-passenger autonomous vehicle without a steering wheel or pedals, which is set for production in 2026 at a price under $30,000. Tesla also unveiled the Robovan, an electric autonomous van designed to transport up to 20 passengers. Meanwhile, Baidu’s Apollo Go launched its latest-generation robotaxi, the RT6, across multiple cities in China.

CHAPTER 3:
Responsible AI

Overview
Artificial intelligence is now deeply integrated into nearly every aspect of our lives. It
is reshaping sectors like education, finance, and healthcare, where algorithm-driven
insights guide critical decisions. While this shift offers significant benefits, it also brings
with it notable risks. The past year has seen a continued concentration of effort on the
responsible development and deployment of AI systems.
This chapter examines trends in responsible AI (RAI) across several dimensions. It
begins by establishing key RAI definitions before assessing broadly relevant issues
such as AI incidents, standardization challenges in LLM responsibility, and benchmarks
for model factuality and truthfulness. Next, it explores RAI trends within key societal
sectors—industry, academia, and policymaking—and analyzes specific subtopics,
including privacy and data governance, fairness, transparency and explainability,
and security and safety, using benchmarks that illuminate model performance and
highlights of notable research. The chapter concludes with a study of two special RAI
topics: agentic AI and election misinformation.

Chapter Highlights
1. Evaluating AI systems with responsible AI criteria is still uncommon, but new benchmarks are beginning
to emerge. Last year’s AI Index highlighted the lack of standardized RAI benchmarks for LLMs. While this issue persists, new
benchmarks such as HELM Safety and AIR-Bench help to fill this gap.

2. The number of AI incident reports continues to increase. According to the AI Incidents Database, the number of
reported AI-related incidents rose to 233 in 2024—a record high and a 56.4% increase over 2023.

3. Organizations acknowledge RAI risks, but mitigation efforts lag. A McKinsey survey on organizations’ RAI
engagement shows that while many identify key RAI risks, not all are taking active steps to address them. Risks including
inaccuracy, regulatory compliance, and cybersecurity were top of mind for leaders with only 64%, 63%, and 60% of respondents,
respectively, citing them as concerns.

4. Across the globe, policymakers demonstrate a significant interest in RAI. In 2024, global cooperation on AI
governance intensified, with a focus on articulating agreed-upon principles for responsible AI. Several major organizations—
including the OECD, European Union, United Nations, and African Union—published frameworks to articulate key RAI concerns
such as transparency and explainability, and trustworthiness.

5. The data commons is rapidly shrinking. AI models rely on massive amounts of publicly available web data for training.
A recent study found that data use restrictions increased significantly from 2023 to 2024, as many websites implemented new
protocols to curb data scraping for AI training. In actively maintained domains in the C4 common crawl dataset, the proportion
of restricted tokens jumped from 5–7% to 20–33%. This decline has consequences for data diversity, model alignment, and
scalability, and may also lead to new approaches to learning with data constraints.

6. Foundation model research transparency improves, yet more work remains. The updated Foundation
Model Transparency Index—a project tracking transparency in the foundation model ecosystem—revealed that the average
transparency score among major model developers increased from 37% in October 2023 to 58% in May 2024. While these gains
are promising, there is still considerable room for improvement.

7. Better benchmarks for factuality and truthfulness. Earlier benchmarks like HaluEval and TruthfulQA, aimed at
evaluating the factuality and truthfulness of AI models, have failed to gain widespread adoption within the AI community. In
response, newer and more comprehensive evaluations have emerged, such as the updated Hughes Hallucination Evaluation
Model leaderboard, FACTS, and SimpleQA.

8. AI-related election misinformation spread globally, but its impact remains unclear. In 2024, numerous
examples of AI-related election misinformation emerged in more than a dozen countries and across over 10 social media
platforms, including during the U.S. presidential election. However, questions remain about measurable impacts of this problem,
with many expecting misinformation campaigns to have affected elections more profoundly than they did.

9. LLMs trained to be explicitly unbiased continue to demonstrate implicit bias. Many advanced LLMs—
including GPT-4 and Claude 3 Sonnet—were designed with measures to curb explicit biases, but they continue to exhibit
implicit ones. The models disproportionately associate negative terms with Black individuals, more often associate women with
humanities instead of STEM fields, and favor men for leadership roles, reinforcing racial and gender biases in decision making.
Although bias metrics have improved on standard benchmarks, AI model bias remains a pervasive issue.

10. RAI gains attention from academic researchers. The number of RAI papers accepted at leading AI conferences
increased by 28.8%, from 992 in 2023 to 1,278 in 2024, continuing a steady annual rise since 2019. This upward trend highlights
the growing importance of RAI within the AI research community.

chunk-012.context:
This section of the AI Index Report 2025 details advancements in cost-effective self-driving technology, new evaluation benchmarks, and safety comparisons between autonomous and human drivers.

The Baidu Apollo Go RT6 robotaxi carries a price tag of just $30,000 and features a battery-swapping system. This vehicle represents a major step toward making self-driving technology more cost-effective and scalable. As autonomous vehicle costs continue to decline, the adoption of self-driving cars is expected to accelerate. Notable business partnerships have also advanced autonomous technology, including Uber’s collaboration with WeRide—the world’s first publicly listed robotaxi company—to develop an autonomous ride-sharing platform in Abu Dhabi.

In 2024, researchers introduced several new benchmarks to evaluate self-driving capabilities, moving away from restrictive open-loop evaluation methods that often cause autonomous driving models to memorize driving patterns instead of learning to drive authentically. One notable example is nuPlan, developed by Motional. nuPlan is a large-scale autonomous driving dataset designed to test machine-learning-based motion planners. The benchmark includes 1,282 hours of diverse driving scenarios from multiple cities, alongside a simulation and evaluation framework that enables planners’ actions to be tested in closed-loop settings.

Bench2Drive is another new benchmark that addresses the limitations of open-loop testing by providing a comprehensive, realistic, closed-loop testing simulation environment for end-to-end autonomous vehicles (Figure 2.9.13). It includes a training set with over 2 million fully annotated frames sourced from more than 10,000 clips, as well as an evaluation suite with 220 short routes designed to test autonomous driving capabilities in diverse conditions. Figure 2.9.14 displays the driving scores of various autonomous driving methods evaluated on the Bench2Drive benchmark. The driving score accounts for both route completion and infractions, averaging route completion percentages while applying penalties based on infraction severity.

OpenAD is a recent benchmark that serves as the first real-world, open-world autonomous driving benchmark specifically for 3D object detection. OpenAD focuses on domain generalization—the ability of autonomous driving systems to adapt across diverse sensor configurations—and open-vocabulary recognition, which allows systems to identify previously unseen semantic categories.

Emerging research on self-driving car safety compares Waymo vehicles to human-driven vehicles in Phoenix and San Francisco. Figure 2.9.15 compares the number of reported incidents per million miles driven by Waymo vehicles to the estimated rates if humans had driven the same distance. The data shows that Waymo vehicles recorded significantly fewer incidents, including 1.42 fewer airbag deployments, 3.16 fewer crashes with reported injuries, and 3.65 fewer police-reported crashes per million miles driven. Figure 2.9.16 highlights the differences in incident rates across various crash locations, revealing that across all locations with available data, Waymo vehicles consistently recorded lower rates of airbag deployments, injury-reported crashes, and police-reported incidents.

Additionally, Waymo collaborated with Swiss Re, one of the world’s leading reinsurers, to conduct a study analyzing liability claims related to collisions over several million miles driven by its fully autonomous vehicles. The study compared Waymo’s liability claims to human-driver baselines derived from Swiss Re’s extensive dataset, which includes over 500,000 claims and 200 billion miles of driving data. The results showed that Waymo vehicles had an 88% reduction in property damage claims and a 92% reduction in bodily injury claims. In real terms, across 25.3 million miles driven, Waymo vehicles were involved in just nine property damage claims and two bodily injury claims, whereas human drivers over the same distance would be expected to incur 78 property damage claims and 26 bodily injury claims. Furthermore, Waymo drivers were significantly safer than latest-generation human-driven vehicles that are equipped with added safety features. Figure 2.9.17 presents a comparison of liability insurance claims by type between the Waymo driver and human-driven vehicles.
chunk-012.summary: The Baidu Apollo Go RT6 robotaxi and Uber-WeRide partnerships highlight cost-effective scaling, while new benchmarks like nuPlan, Bench2Drive, and OpenAD shift evaluation toward closed-loop and real-world testing. Safety data from Waymo in Phoenix and San Francisco shows 1.42 fewer airbag deployments, 3.16 fewer injury crashes, and 3.65 fewer police-reported crashes per million miles compared to humans, alongside an 88% property damage and 92% bodily injury claim reduction per Swiss Re.
